title: Fiber Photometry Signal Characterization Automation
text:
Fiber photometry is a commonly used technique to record in vivo neural activity and neurotransmitter dynamics. Fiber photometry requires the expression of a fluorescent sensor and the implantation of a fiber optic cannula through which changes in fluorescence can be measured in real time. Surgical success rates vary and the classification of subjects with real biological signal is critical to maintaining the quality of collected data sets, which is critical for robust, replicable, and interpretable scientific findings. Subjective assessment of signal presence and quality presents a challenge both in the determination of data inclusion criteria and in consistency between researchers.
The goal of this analysis was to enable automatic classification of individual subject fiber photometry recordings and identify subjects with biological signal versus those lacking biological signal. To do so, I applied an elastic net logistic regression model to establish a robust classification threshold for predicting the presence of a true signal based on extracted features.

title: Fiber Photometry Signal Characterization Automation
text:
Methods
All subjects in this data set were prepared for other experimental protocols. Recordings were conducted prior to the start of experimental protocols.

Surgical Preparation
Subjects were prepared for fiber photometry experiments with injection of viral vectors to express one of three fluorescent constructs: GCaMP6f in ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine (DA) cell bodies (TH:CRE rat line), dLight1.3b in the nucleus accumbens (NAc; lateral shell or core), or GRABDA2H in the NAc (lateral shell or core). Subjects were monitored postoperatively for a minimum of 10 days.


Fiber Photometry Recordings
Fiber photometry recordings were conducted a minimum of three weeks post-surgery to allow for stabilization of sensor expression. Recordings were conducted in standard operant conditioning chambers (house light and fan on) with RZ5 or RZ10 processors and the software Synapse (Tucker Davis Technologies). Sensor-dependent signal was measured via a 465 nm LED, while a control stream was recorded via a 405 nm LED. A minimum of 5 minutes of recording was collected for each subject.


Signal Classification
Fiber photometry recordings were hand scored as having ‘Signal’ or ‘No Signal’ based on prior experience and subjective evaluation. Recordings were also assigned a quality score from 0 to 4, with 0 meaning no signal, 1 meaning low quality signal that should be classified as no signal, 2 meaning moderate signal of sufficient quality to be scored as having signal, and 3 meaning high quality signal.
Each recording was scored two times independently, and discrepancies were reconciled based on the signal quality ratings assigned in both scores.


Signal Processing
Fiber photometry data were extracted and processed in MATLAB (2026a) as in Donka et al, 2025. Briefly, raw data streams were extracted. The background stream (405nm) was scaled to the signal stream (465nm) based on a constant factor derived from the ratio of the power within a high frequency band optimized by sensor (e.g., 10 to 100 Hz). The subtracted data stream was produced by subtracting the scaled background from the raw signal to control for photobleaching and motion artifact effects. The final filtered data stream was produced by applying a band pass Butterworth filter (High pass: 0.0051 Hz; Low pass: 5 Hz) to the subtracted data stream.


Feature Quantification
For feature quantification, fiber photometry streams were divided into halves (2.5 minutes each), and variables were quantified for each 30 second bin within the separated recordings. Averages across bins were calculated to provide one estimate for each recording.
Fiber photometry recordings were quantified by a variety of parameters including stream range, root mean squared (RMS), mean, and power spectrum magnitude (low, medium, and high frequency bands). Quantification was performed for raw signal, raw background, scaled background, subtracted signal, and subtracted and filtered streams. Additionally, ratios between values in subtracted and scaled background streams were included across variables.
Quantified variables were exported to a .csv file and all further analysis was conducted in R.

Code
## Read in data and prep variables -----
subjectvariables <- read_csv(paste(rootboxpath, 'Roitman Data Repository/Projects/2026_FPSignalCharacterizationAutomation_RD/Analysis/', 'FPSignalCharacterizationAutomation_ExperimentalVariables.csv',sep=''))
data_raw <- read_csv(paste(rootboxpath, 'Roitman Data Repository/Projects/2026_FPSignalCharacterizationAutomation_RD/Analysis/', 'FPSignalCharacterizationAutomation_AllQuantificationVariables.csv',sep=''))

# Merge subject variables with data
data <- left_join(data_raw, subjectvariables, by = "SubjectID")  %>% filter(Sensor != 'GRABDA3M')

set.seed(123)

# Create subject-level summary for stratification
subject_summary <- data %>%
  group_by(SubjectID, Sensor) %>%
  summarise(
    Signal = first(Signal_RDScored),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Stratified sample of Subjects
train_subjects <- subject_summary %>%
  group_by(Sensor, Signal) %>%
  sample_frac(0.5) %>%
  pull(SubjectID)

# Assign Set based on SubjectID
data_split <- data %>%
  mutate(Set = ifelse(SubjectID %in% train_subjects, "Train", "Test"))

# Pivot data to wide
data_wide <- data_split %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(SubjectID, Split, Set, Sex, FiberPlacement, Sensor, Rig, Power, Signal_RDScored, Signal_RDQuality, baqscalingfactor),
    names_from = Variable,
    values_from = c(sig, baq, baqscaled, sigsub, sigfilt, sigtobaq, sigtobaqscaled)
  )

# Factor categorical variables
data_wide$Split <- factor(data_wide$Split)
data_wide$Sex <- factor(data_wide$Sex)
data_wide$FiberPlacement <- factor(data_wide$FiberPlacement, levels=c('VTA','NAcLS'))
data_wide$Sensor <- factor(data_wide$Sensor, levels=c('GCaMP6f','GRABDA2H','dLight1.3b'))
data_wide$Rig <- factor(data_wide$Rig)
data_wide$Signal <- factor(data_wide$Signal_RDScored, levels=c('N','Y'))
data_wide$SignalQuality <- factor(data_wide$Signal_RDQuality)


# Scale ratios
data_wide$sigtobaq_mean_bins_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaq_mean_bins-1
data_wide$sigtobaq_range_bins_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaq_range_bins-1
data_wide$sigtobaq_rms_bins_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaq_rms_bins-1

data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_mean_bins_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_mean_bins-1

data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_rms_bins_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_rms_bins-1

data_wide$sigtobaq_MagSum_Band3_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaq_MagSum_Band3-1

data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band1_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band1-1
data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band2_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band2-1
data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band3_scaled <- data_wide$sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band3-1

## Analysis Variables -----
IDvariables <- c('SubjectID','Sensor','Set','Split','Signal','SignalQuality')

includevariables <- c('sig_range_bins', 'sig_rms_bins', 'sig_MagSum_Band1', 'sig_MagSum_Band2','sig_MagSum_Band3',
                      'baq_range_bins', 'baq_rms_bins', 'baq_MagSum_Band1', 'baq_MagSum_Band2','baq_MagSum_Band3',
                      'baqscaled_range_bins', 'baqscaled_rms_bins', 'baqscaled_MagSum_Band1', 'baqscaled_MagSum_Band2','baqscaled_MagSum_Band3',
                      'sigsub_range_bins', 'sigsub_rms_bins', 'sigsub_MagSum_Band1', 'sigsub_MagSum_Band2','sigsub_MagSum_Band3',
                      'sigfilt_range_bins', 'sigfilt_rms_bins', 'sigfilt_MagSum_Band1', 'sigfilt_MagSum_Band2',
                      'sigtobaq_rms_bins_scaled','sigtobaq_MagSum_Band1_scaled', 'sigtobaq_MagSum_Band2_scaled', 'sigtobaq_MagSum_Band3_scaled',
                      'sigtobaqscaled_rms_bins_scaled','sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band1_scaled', 'sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band2_scaled', 'sigtobaqscaled_MagSum_Band3_scaled')

includevariables_labels <- c('Raw Signal Range', 'Raw Signal RMS', 'Raw Signal Low Freq FFT Mag', 'Raw Signal Medium Freq FFT Mag','Raw Signal High Freq FFT Mag',
                             'Raw Background Range', 'Raw Background RMS', 'Raw Background Low Freq FFT Mag', 'Raw Background Medium Freq FFT Mag','Raw Background High Freq FFT Mag',
                             'Scaled Background Range', 'Scaled Background RMS', 'Scaled Background Low Freq FFT Mag', 'Scaled Background Medium Freq FFT Mag','Scaled Background High Freq FFT Mag',                      
                             'Subtracted Signal Range', 'Subtracted Signal RMS', 'Subtracted Signal Low Freq FFT Mag', 'Subtracted Signal Medium Freq FFT Mag','Subtracted Signal High Freq FFT Mag',
                             'Filtered Signal Range', 'Filtered Signal RMS', 'Filtered Signal Low Freq FFT Mag', 'Filtered Signal Medium Freq FFT Mag',
                             'Raw Signal:Raw Background RMS', 'Raw Signal:Raw Background Low Freq FFT Mag', 'Raw Signal:Raw Background Medium Freq FFT Mag','Raw Signal:Raw Background High Freq FFT Mag',

title: Fiber Photometry Signal Characterization Automation
text:
Model Specification: Elastic Net Classification
To classify whether fiber photometry recordings contained a biological signal (Y/N), an Elastic Net logistic regression was trained. Elastic Net applies a combination of Ridge (L2) and Lasso (L1) penalities (\(\alpha = 0.5\)) to handle correlated predictors while inherently performing feature selection.
The model was trained on the following structure:
Predictors (Features): 30 extracted signal metrics, encompassing raw, background-subtracted, and scaled variables across amplitude and frequency domains.
Target (Outcome): The binary `Signal` variable (Yes / No).
Validation: The dataset was partitioned into training and testing sets using a stratified split, ensuring that signal classifications and sensor types (e.g., GCaMP6f, dLight1.3b) were equally balanced across both sets. To identify the optimal regularization parameter (lambda), the model utilized 10-fold cross-validation on the training set. The final model was evaluated on the test set, converting predicted probabilities into binary classifications using a standard 0.5 decision threshold.


Code
# ELASTIC NET - SIGNAL -----
## Prepare train and test data -----
# Remove extra columns
ENdata <- modeldata

# Create training and testing sets
ENdata_train <- ENdata %>% filter(Set == "Train") %>% select(-Set, -Split)
ENdata_test  <- ENdata %>% filter(Set == "Test")%>% select(-Set, -Split)

# Create design matrix of predictors (excluding SubjectID)
EN_x_train <- model.matrix(~ . -1 -Signal -SignalQuality -SubjectID -Sensor, data = ENdata_train)
EN_y_train <- ENdata_train$Signal

# Prepare test
EN_x_test <- model.matrix(~ . -1 -Signal -SignalQuality -SubjectID-Sensor, data = ENdata_test)
EN_y_test <- ENdata_test$Signal

## Fit elastic net -----
set.seed(123)

EN_cv <- cv.glmnet(
  x = EN_x_train,
  y = EN_y_train,
  family = "binomial",
  alpha = 0.5,             
  type.measure = "class",
  nfolds = 10 # 10-fold cross-validation
)

# Set lambda 
EN_minlambda <- EN_cv$lambda.min

# Refit model at this lambda
EN_finalmodel <- glmnet(EN_x_train, EN_y_train, family = "binomial", alpha = 0.5, lambda = EN_minlambda)

## Predict test set -----
# Predict probabilities
EN_test_probs <- predict(EN_finalmodel, newx = EN_x_test, type = "response")

# Convert to binary predictions using threshold of 0.5
EN_test_preds <- ifelse(EN_test_probs > 0.5, "Y", "N") %>% factor(levels = c("N", "Y"))

# Predict class
EN_pred_class <- predict(EN_cv, newx = EN_x_test, s = "lambda.min", type = "class")

# Predict probability
EN_pred_prob <- predict(EN_cv, newx = EN_x_test, s = "lambda.min", type = "response")

# Confusion matrix
EN_confusion <- table(Predicted = EN_test_preds, Actual = EN_y_test)

accuracy <- mean(EN_test_preds == EN_y_test)


# Extract coefficients
EN_coef <- coef(EN_finalmodel) %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
  rename(coefficient = `s0`) %>%
  filter(coefficient != 0 & variable != "(Intercept)")


EN_coef_cleaned <- EN_coef %>%
  mutate(abs_coef = abs(coefficient),
         Direction = ifelse(coefficient > 0, "Predicts Signal", "Predicts No Signal"),
         Signal = ifelse(coefficient > 0, "Y", "N")) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_coef)) %>%
  slice(1:30) # Select top predictors


variable_lookup <- setNames(includevariables_labels, includevariables)

EN_coef_cleaned <- EN_coef %>% filter(variable != "X.Intercept.") %>%
  mutate(abs_coef = abs(coefficient),
         Direction = ifelse(coefficient > 0, "Predicts Signal", "Predicts No Signal"),
         Signal = ifelse(coefficient > 0, "Y", "N")) %>%
  mutate(variablename = coalesce(variable_lookup[variable], variable)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(abs_coef)) %>%
  slice(1:30)


# Rank byVariableNames2String()# Rank by absolute value
EN_toppredictors <- EN_coef %>%
  mutate(abs_coef = abs(coefficient)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs_coef))


## ADD BACK CATEGORICAL ID VARIABLES -----
catvars <- data_wide %>% filter(Split == 1)

EN_data_test_full <- ENdata_test %>%
  left_join(catvars %>% select(SubjectID, FiberPlacement, Power, Rig),
            by = c("SubjectID"))

EN_test_results <- EN_data_test_full %>%
  select(SubjectID, Signal, SignalQuality, Sensor, FiberPlacement, SignalQuality, Power, Rig) %>%
  mutate(
    Predicted = EN_test_preds,
    Prob_Y = as.numeric(EN_test_probs),
    Correct = (Signal == EN_test_preds)
  )

EN_test_results$SensorSignalQuality <- paste(EN_test_results$Sensor, EN_test_results$SignalQuality, sep='_')

## SUMMARIZE -----
EN_test_results_summary_quality <- EN_test_results %>%
  group_by(Sensor, Signal, SignalQuality, SensorSignalQuality) %>%
  summarise(
    Accuracy = mean(Correct),
    AccuracyPerc = scales::percent(mean(Correct), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = n(),
    n_correct = sum(Correct),
    n_incorrect = n - n_correct,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#EN_test_results_summary_quality

EN_test_results_summary <- EN_test_results %>%
  group_by(Sensor, Signal) %>%
  summarise(
    Accuracy = mean(Correct),
    AccuracyPerc = scales::percent(mean(Correct), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = n(),
    n_correct = sum(Correct),
    n_incorrect = n - n_correct,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: Fiber Photometry Signal Characterization Automation
text:
Model Results
Overall, the specified elastic net model successfully characterized fiber photometry recordings into ‘Signal’ and ‘No Signal’ categories based on quantified parameters extracted from the data streams. Model accuracy was 89.91%. Of the 32 variables included in the model, 23 were significant predictors of Signal or No Signal classifications.

Optimal Regularization Parameter
To identify the optimal regularization parameter (lambda) for the model, 10-fold cross-validation was performed on the training data set. Penalties exceeding the the threshold (lambda.min) resulted in an increase in misclassification. The lambda min value was used to finalize model weights.


Code
## FIGURE 1: CV error curve
cv_data <- tibble(
  lambda = EN_cv$lambda,
  log_lambda = log(EN_cv$lambda),
  cvm = EN_cv$cvm, # Cross-validation mean error
  cvsd = EN_cv$cvsd, # Cross-validation standard deviation
  cvup = EN_cv$cvup, # Upper bound of error curve
  cvlo = EN_cv$cvlo, # Lower bound of error curve
  nzero = EN_cv$nzero # Number of non-zero coefficients
)

log_lambda_min <- log(EN_cv$lambda.min)

fig_cv_error <- ggplot(cv_data, aes(x = log_lambda, y = cvm)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = cvlo, ymax = cvup), color = "#707070", width = 0.06) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log_lambda_min, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = log_lambda_min, y = max(cv_data$cvup), 
           label = "Lambda", angle = 90, vjust = -0.5, hjust=.8, color = "red", size=6) +
  labs(
    title = "Elastic Net Cross-Validation Error",
    subtitle = "Performance across regularization penalties",
    x = "Log(Lambda)",
    y = "Misclassification Error") +
  mytheme +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

fig_cv_error









Figure 1: Elastic Net Cross-Validation Error. 10-fold cross-validation performance across a sequence of regularization penalties (\(\lambda\)). Error bars represent one standard deviation. The red dashed line indicates the optimal penalty (lambda.min) that minimizes classification error.


Variable Importance
Non-predictive coefficients were forced to zero and therefore excluded from the model. After exclusion, 23 of 32 coefficients remained. Overall, frequency domain features were the most predictive of accurate classification, with the strongest positive predictors of a physiological signal being the ratio of the FFT magnitude ratios of the raw signal to the scaled background. Conversely, the ratio of the RMS of the raw signal to the scaled background was the strongest negative predictor.


Code
# FIGURE 2: Variable Importance
fig_m1_variable_importance <- EN_coef_cleaned %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = coefficient, y = fct_reorder(variablename, coefficient), fill = Signal)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors_signal, labels = c("Predicts No Signal","Predicts Signal")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Top Variables (Signal vs. No Signal)",
       subtitle = paste("Elastic Net (\u03B1=0.5)"),
       x = "Elastic Net Coefficient", y = "") +
  mytheme_legend +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linewidth = myaxislinewidth, linetype = 'dashed',color='black')

fig_m1_variable_importance









Figure 2: Variable Importance from the Elastic Net Classification Model. Non-zero coefficients extracted from the optimized elastic net model.


Model Accuracy
To evaluate model performance across all classification thresholds, a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was conducted on the test data set. Model AUC was 0.957, indicating strong performance. The model successfully maximized sensitivity (accurate ‘Yes’ signal classifications), while maintaining a high degree of specificity (accurate ‘No’ signal classifications).
Categorical predictions were generated using a standard 0.5 decision threshold. The confusion matrix supports high global accuracy of 89.91%. Total classification errors were balanced between ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ signal categorizations, indicating a low level of bias in the automatic classification. Predicted probabilities displayed a bi-modal distribution, indicating a low volume of ambiguous classifications.


Code
# FIGURE 3A: ROC Curve
roc_obj <- roc(EN_y_test, as.numeric(EN_test_probs))
auc_value <- round(auc(roc_obj), 3)

fig_m1_roc <- ggroc(roc_obj, color = colors_signal_Y, size = 1.2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth=myaxislinewidth) +
  labs(title = paste("Signal Model Performance: AUC =", auc_value),
       subtitle = "Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)",
       x = "Specificity (Correct 'No Signal' classification)", y = "Sensitivity (Correct 'Yes Signal' Classification)") +
  mytheme



# FIGURE 3B: Confusion Matrix Heatmap
en_cm_tidy <- EN_confusion %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(Actual = factor(Actual, levels=rev(levels(Actual))),
         Predicted = factor(Predicted, levels=levels(Predicted)))

fig_m1_confusion_matrix <- en_cm_tidy %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 8, color = "black")+
  scale_fill_gradient(low = colors_signal_N, high = colors_signal_Y, name = "Count") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(title = "Confusion Matrix",
       x = "Predicted", y = "Actual") +
  mytheme_legend + theme(legend.position = 'right')


# FIGURE 3C: Probability Density (Calibration Check)
fig_m1_probability_density <- EN_test_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Prob_Y, fill = Signal)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 1, color=NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = myaxislinewidth, color = "black") + # Classification threshold
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("N" = colors_signal_N, "Y" = colors_signal_Y), name = "Actual Signal") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0), limits = c(0,10), breaks=seq(0,10,2.5)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Probability vs. Actual Classification",
       x = "Predicted Probability of Signal (Prob Y)", y = "Density") +
  mytheme_legend +
  theme(legend.position = "right")



plot_grid(fig_m1_roc, fig_m1_confusion_matrix, fig_m1_probability_density,
          ncol = 3, nrow=1, align = "hv",
          axis  = "tblr", hjust=-.5, labels = "AUTO")









Figure 3: Elastic Net Model Signal Classification Accuracy. A) ROC analysis of the elastic net model indicating high sensitivity and specificity in signal classification. B) Confusion matrix of test set predictions (0.5 probability threshold). C) Probability density of model predictions on the test data set grouped by hand-scored signal classification.


Effect of Signal Quality on Signal Classification
To determine if classification errors were driven by signal quality, model accuracy was evaluated across hand-scored signal quality scores (0-3; 0-1 = ‘No Signal’, 2-3 = ‘Signal’). Incorrect classifications decreased as signal quality increased, with the greatest number of incorrect classifications occurring with signal quality ratings of 2, which reflect fiber photometry recordings where signal was evaluated to be visible but mid quality (Fig. 4A). Across signal quality ratings, relative accuracy was above 80%, and reacher 99% for signal quality ratings of 3 (Fig. 4B). The variance of predicted probabilities was greatest across recordings with a signal quality score of 2.
To statistically test differences in model performance across signal quality scores, I performed a binomial logistic regression (Correct ~ Signal Quality) and Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons, which indicated significant differences in accuracy between recordings with signal quality scores of 0 vs 3 and 2 vs 3. No other differences in accuracy between quality ratings were observed.

Figure 4. Classification Outcomes by Signal Quality. Overall, signal quality significantly affected the accuracy of classification. A) Classification outcomes in the test data set by signal quality ratings. 0 = no observable signs of sensor-dependent fluorescence; 1 = minor observable signs of sensor-dependent fluorescence but not sufficient to classify as having signal; 2 = observable signal of moderate quality with small to moderate visible fluctuations in sensor-dependent fluorescence; 3 = observable and high quality signal with large visible fluctuations in fluorescence. B) Relative model accuracy (percent correct classification) by signal quality scores. The model achieved > 80% accuracy across all signal quality ratings, with 99% accuracy for high quality recordings (Signal Quality = 3). C) Boxplots of the distributions of predicted probabilities across signal quality scores. Solid horizontal lines represent median probabilities with statistical outliers displayed as points.


Effect of Sensor on Signal Classification
To determine if sensor type (VTA GCaMP6f, NAc dLight1.3b, or NAc GRABDA2H) significantly affected model accuracy, signal classification in the test set was stratified by sensor type. Overall, accuracy was comparable across sensors and well exceeded the 50% threshold of random chance, with the lowest accuracy percent at 87.5% for GRABDA2H (Fig. 5A).
Absolute values of counts of incorrect and correct model predictions were statistically compared. No significant effect of sensor was revealed by Fisher’s Exact Test for Count Data (Fig. 5B). Evaluation of the distributions of predicted probabilities by sensor indicated reliable predictions of both ‘No Signal’ and ‘Signal’ across all three sensors, but the distribution of predictions for GRABDA2H ‘No Signal’ recordings was wider than for GCaMP6f and dLight1.3b (Fig. 5C).
Model performance across signal quality ratings was highly comparable across sensors, with the highest level of accuracy observed for signal quality scores of 3. Accuracy was lower for GRABDA2H recordings with signal quality scores of 0, potentially driven by a greater degree of sensitivity to DA binding or extended temporal kinetics relative to GCaMP6f and dLight1.3b. However, the decreased accuracy with GRABDA2H in recordings of signal quality 0 was still significantly above chance (Fig. 5D). Decision thresholds may be optimally tailored by sensor to mitigate the incorrect classification of data streams without signal via increasing the strictness of the predicted probability threshold for ‘Yes’ signal classification.
Together, these results indicate that the included predictors capture reliable profiles that can be applied to classify fiber photometry recordings of in vivo DA activity independent of individual sensor kinetics.
